title: Nine Tenths Underfoot
question: What are silicate minerals, and what decides their colour?
hook: Almost all of the crust beneath you belongs to a single family of minerals.
idea: Silicate minerals, built from silicon-oxygen groups balanced by metal ions, make up about 90 percent of Earth's crust and owe their colours to those metals.

beats.prompt: A silicate mineral contains a lot of iron. Which of its features is the iron most likely to shape?

choices.label: Whether it counts as a silicate
choices.feedback: It is still a silicate; the metal sits alongside the silicate groups to balance their charge.

choices.label: Whether silicon is surrounded by four oxides
choices.feedback: Most silicates have silicon among four oxides; the metal's visible effect is colour.

beats.explain: Silicate groups are colourless; the colours of silicate minerals come from the metal component, commonly iron.

beats.prompt: Sort each into its role in a silicate mineral.
beats.explain: The silicate subunits are made of silicon and oxygen, and metal cations such as Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Na⁺ balance their charge.
Silica sits in different classes depending on the system, living diatoms use it for shells, and iron is the usual colouring metal.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Diatoms are a type of plankton
Diatoms build shells from silica taken from seawater
The shells of dead diatoms are a major part of deep ocean sediment
So living things play no part in the cycle that forms silicates
beats.explain: Living organisms do contribute to this geologic cycle, and diatoms are the example: their silica shells pile up as sediment.
